title: On Interpretation, Part 9 (the sea-battle chapter)
version: E. M. Edghill translation, hosted by MIT Internet Classics Archive; Part 9 of the translation. Bekker location 18b23 ff. as given by Øhrstrøm & Hasle (SEP, rev. 2024); the translation itself displays no Bekker numbers.
locator: Part 9 in its entirety, read directly: the fatalist argument from bivalence, the fortuitous/inevitable claim, the deliberation remark, and Aristotle's own two-sided-potentiality resolution.
assumptions: Propositions have truth-values; for what is or has taken place bivalence holds; chance concerns events whose reality may issue in either of two directions.
conclusion: For future events with potentiality in contrary directions it is necessary that either the event or its negation will occur, but not necessary determinately that this one occur; one member may be more likely, yet neither is actually true or actually false now; otherwise deliberation would be pointless.
proof_status: Primary text; interpretation contested in the literature (Markosian 1995: 'it at least appears' Aristotle endorses the gap move).
open_questions: Which of the modern positions Aristotle actually endorses remains disputed; not needed for this lane beyond the argument's shape.
relevance: Origin of the fatalist argument the whole area answers; source of the deliberation-action link between truth and agency.
limits: Outdated public-domain translation (Edghill); modern translations (e.g. Ackrill) not consulted; Bekker pagination attributed via the SEP entry, not verified against a critical edition.

title: Future Contingents
version: First published 9 June 2011; substantive revision 11 July 2024.
locator: Whole entry read: §1 ancient/medieval background incl. Lavenham's 9-step argument and four reactions; §2 formal reconstruction with principles P1-P5; §3 branching time and the Kripke 1958 letter; §4.1-4.2 Łukasiewicz and Peircean clauses; §5.1-5.5 Ockhamist, Leibnizian, true-futurist/TRL (TRL1, TRL2, TRL2'), supervaluationist and relativist clauses; §6 classification table; bibliography.
assumptions: Presented as exposition, not as defended theses.
conclusion: Solutions divide by whether they reject future excluded middle (P5) or the necessity of the past (P3), and by whether future contingents have chronicle-independent truth-values; 2x2 classification table given.
proof_status: Secondary exposition of others' formal systems; truth clauses copied clause-by-clause with Prior/Thomason locators.
open_questions: Whether any important theory rejects both P3 and P5 (entry says none known to its authors).
relevance: Scaffold for positions and the canonical argument's formal shape; source of the Kripke-letter branching origin and Thomason's substitution objection (p. 280 as cited there).
limits: Secondary; page references to paywalled primaries (Prior 1967; Thomason 1970) are taken on the entry's authority, not verified.

title: Future Contingents and Relative Truth
version: Author offprint of the paper in The Philosophical Quarterly 53 (212), July 2003; winner of the PQ Essay Prize 2002 (stated on the offprint). Page footers on the offprint run pp. 326-332 for the sections read; journal pagination 321-336 recorded by secondary sources, not independently verified.
locator: §I problem and the two intuitions; §II-III standard solutions surveyed (skimmed); §IV absoluteness of utterance-truth (read); §V semantics proper (Will/Sett clauses), supervaluational and thin-red-line postsemantics, and the double-time-reference postsemantics with the m0/m1/m2 verdicts (read); §VI Evans' challenge and the reply (read); §VII assertion (not read to the end).
assumptions: Branching-time semantics proper with moment/history points; Will shifts along a history; Sett quantifies over histories through a moment.
conclusion: Utterance-truth must be relativized to a context of assessment: the sea-battle utterance is neither true nor false as assessed when made, true as assessed from the battle, false as assessed from no battle; this respects both the indeterminacy and determinacy intuitions at the cost of a-contextuality.
proof_status: Formal semantics with postsemantics; internally consistent as presented; the author himself superseded the 2003 argument's formulation in later work (recorded by this repository's retrospection lane).
open_questions: Assertion norms under a-contextuality (§VII and the later book); whether the framework's neutrality about a-contextual sentences is exploited by any other operator.
relevance: Primary source for assessment relativism; defines the third truth policy missing from main.tex's L/S menu.
limits: §VII on assertion not read to the end; the author's own later revision (2007/2008 chapter; 2014 book) not read here; offprint lacks journal page anchors for §I-V.

title: Branching space-time (postprint January 2003)
version: Postprint dated 11 February 2003 of Belnap 1992, 'Branching space-time', Synthese 92 (1992) 385-434, DOI 10.1007/BF00414289 (original's DOI verified from the Springer record). The postprint's own footnote +1 directs that it be quoted under its present title and date, with an indication that it is unpublished.
locator: Whole postprint read (51 pp.): §2 postulates incl. 2-1 partial order and no backward branching; §3 Def 3-2 histories as maximal directed subsets, 3-4 compatibility, 3-8 space-like separation; §4 historical connection (4-1) and the M property (4-3); §5 Def 5-1 obviously undivided, 5-2 finest partition Π_e, 5-6 indeterministic point events, 5-7/5-8 choice points maximal in h1∩h2; §6-7 choice principle (6-1) and prior choice principle (7-1); §8 wings problem, Fact 8-3 wings in the intersection; §9 indeterminism without choice; §10 splitting along a slice; §11 EPR proposal and conjectures; §12 summary; §13 appendix: 13-1 prior choice for chains, infima/suprema/density postulates, Fact 13-11 transitivity, Fact 13-15 'yes and no' (point vs chain determination).
assumptions: Our World of possible point events with causal order ≤; no backward branching; histories maximal directed.
conclusion: Indeterminism and relativity combine: splitting occurs at point events, not simultaneity slices, and affects only the causal future; the entire proper past of a point determines its occurrence, while the entire past of a last-member-less chain need not determine what comes next.
proof_status: Postulates, definitions and elementary facts with arguments given in the document; elementary order theory, no probability structure built in (Weiner's constructive suggestions noted in its references as unpublished).
open_questions: Probabilities on Π_e (Weiner); transfer of the history definition to GR (taken up by Placek 2014 and BMP 2021, read by this repository's relativistic-branching lane).
relevance: Primary source for branching time's relativistic descendant; Fact 13-15 is the order-theoretic analogue of the paper's pointed-base vs slice-base distinction; verifies main.tex Part II's claim that its guarantee notion is not Belnap's.
limits: Read in postprint form, which the author says may differ from the 1992 original without explicit notice; page numbers cited here are postprint-internal, not Synthese pagination.

title: The Open Past
version: Author copy headed 'A version of this paper appears in Philosophical Studies 79 (1995), pp. 95-105'.
locator: Whole paper read: the Montana-lunch fatalist argument with premises (1)-(4); the open-future response defined via failure of bivalence at a time; the three question-begging defences rejected; the positive defence from nomic indeterminism plus TCT; the time-symmetry argument (Figures 1-2) for indeterminism with regard to the past; the open-past conclusion and the two morals; footnotes 5-15 incl. the McCall and Łukasiewicz attributions.
assumptions: Truth-value status relativized to times; falsity must be contrariety, not contradiction, for stable gaps (n. 7); truths about laws count as truths about the present state (n. 8).
conclusion: The only plausible, non-question-begging defence of the open future response appeals to indeterministic laws plus the tensed correspondence theory of truth (p true at t iff p corresponds to the world at t); since (mostly) time-symmetric indeterministic laws are also indeterministic toward the past, that defence forces the conclusion that the past is sometimes open (as a possibility, with an empirical premise for actuality).
proof_status: Philosophical argument, not a formal theorem; qualifications stated in footnotes 9 and 13.
dependencies: van Inwagen, An Essay on Free Will ch. II
open_questions: Whether a correspondence-now requirement can be motivated without begging against bivalence-preserving rivals; whether time-symmetric indeterminism actually obtains (his footnote 11 restricts to processes both indeterministic and reversible).
relevance: Directly bears on this repository's fixing-exchange note: its Proposition 4 is a fixing-side analogue of Markosian's truth-side argument, but the two connect only through a truth policy; the note's credit line must be qualified.
limits: Author copy, not the journal PDF; journal pagination visible only in the header line.

title: The Truth About the Past and the Future
version: Author copy headed 'A version of this paper appears in Fabrice Correia and Andrea Iacona (eds.), Around the Tree: Semantic and Metaphysical Issues Concerning Branching Time and the Open Future (Springer, 2013), pp. 127-141'; chapter DOI 10.1007/978-94-007-5167-5_8 as recorded by secondary listings (not verified against the publisher page).
locator: §§1-6 read: presentism and the truthmaker problem; the branching-time solution (truth now determined by present things plus laws, deterministic laws giving truth, indeterministic giving gaps); the P1F1 glitch (a model where P1F1φ is false at a point where φ is true); the route-based repair; objections and replies sections (read in part).
assumptions: Presentism; truthmaker principle; branching models with backward branching allowed where laws are past-indeterministic.
conclusion: A branching semantics with routes solves the truthmaker problem for presentism and forces models with past-branching wherever the laws are indeterministic toward the past.
proof_status: Semantic clauses with a small-model illustration; no formal soundness proof claimed.
open_questions: Whether route-based truth conditions survive relativistic spacetime structure (not addressed).
relevance: Connects the open-past argument (1995) to truthmaker grounding, i.e. to this repository's future-truth-grounding lane; a fourth option in the grounding problem alongside TCT, laws-as-truthmakers and metaphysical indeterminacy.
limits: Some objection/reply sections read only in part; publisher page not independently checked.

title: The Incompatibility of Free Will and Determinism
kind: primary philosophical research (copy hosted on an LSE teaching page)
version: Philosophical Studies 27 (1975) 185-199 (journal line printed on the file's page footers); received 18 March 1974. DOI not visible on the copy.
locator: Part I definition of determinism (state-propositions plus laws entailment, with two restrictions on 'state'); Part II 'can' and the render-false idiom; Part III the judge case and the seven-step main argument, with per-premise defences (premises 4 and 5 as instances of two 'analytic' transfer principles; premise 6 via the law/falsifiability conceptual claim); Part IV replies: the criteria argument, the free-will-entails-determinism argument, the conditional analysis dilemma.
assumptions: Determinism as defined; ability talk via 'could have rendered false'; laws not renderable false by anyone.
conclusion: If determinism is true, no agent could have done otherwise (in the sense at issue); incompatibilism.
proof_status: The argument's validity is truth-functional given premise (2); the contest is over the premises; the 1983 book recasts the argument with operators N and rule β (not read here).
open_questions: The standing objections: Lewis 1981 local miracles; Slote 1982 context-sensitivity of unavoidability; rule β counterexamples in the 1983 formulation.
Whether the transfer principles are analytic is the crux the literature disputes.
relevance: The canonical consequence argument; supplies the exact determinism notion that main.tex Parts II-III call 'fixing' by base plus law; shows the fatalist and free-will debates share the no-power-over-past-or-laws pattern.
limits: Read from a teaching-page scan of the author copy; not the 1983 book version; no DOI recorded.

title: The Open Future: Bivalence, Determinism and Ontology
version: Author PDF headed 'University of Leeds'; no publication line visible on the copy. Commonly cited as Philosophical Perspectives 25 (2011); that venue was not verified from the accessed file.
locator: §0 introduction and the three commonly drawn consequences (non-bivalence, indeterminism, anti-eternalism); §1a the familiar bivalence argument (steps 1-5) read; §1 middle sections on the precisification semantics skimmed; §2 Determinism read in full: the conditional-necessity argument, 'what is metaphysically necessary is settled' granted for the hardest case, unsettledness in the antecedent via state or (on regularity theories) laws, note 23 on precisifications; §3a Ontology read: Diekemper's inexorability question and the orthogonality reply.
assumptions: Indeterminacy as variance across precisifications (ersatz worlds); no truth-value gaps; determinate truth = true at every precisification (their stated attraction: excluded middle and bivalence come out determinately true).
conclusion: The open future thesis is compatible with unrestricted bivalence, with deterministic laws, and with eternalist ontology; determinism makes only a conditional metaphysically necessary, and openness survives wherever there is unsettledness in the conditional's antecedent.
proof_status: Philosophical argument; the determinism argument is explicitly conditional on the settlement-of-necessities premise they grant for the hardest case.
open_questions: Whether their precisification story applies symmetrically to past-tensed propositions (the accessed sections raise but do not settle the asymmetry question for their own view); whether S4 must be rejected if necessity itself can be indeterminate (their note 23).
relevance: The pole opposite Markosian in the grounding problem: truth now without present correspondence or future ontology; supplies the determinism/open-future independence result that main.tex's Part IV needs as background.
limits: Publication details not verified from the copy; §1 middle (the bivalence compatibilist machinery) read only in part.

title: Decision and the Open Future
version: Author PDF; in Adrian Bardon (ed.), The Future of the Philosophy of Time, Routledge, pp. 149-168 (page range from the author's listing; printed folios 149-166 visible on the copy).
locator: Whole chapter read: §1 reconstructing temporal phenomenology (Broad, growing block vs branching universe); §2-3 the embedded agent, first/third-person predictive asymmetry (chess example); §4 Wittgenstein and Anscombe on self-knowledge and intention (absence of surprise; self-fulfilling performances); §5 necessity of action (spontaneity vs receptivity; Bennett); the TEv (temporally evolving view) construction; the Anna Karenina three-perspectives passage; conclusion and note 1 crediting the Albert/Horwich/Reichenbach counterfactual-asymmetry story.
assumptions: Physics presents time as one dimension of a manifold; experience is of an embedded participant whose performances are inputs to outcomes.
conclusion: The open future/fixity of past asymmetry is a real feature of the embedded, deliberative perspective - the future is represented as 'unrealized potential' precisely where outcomes depend on one's volitions - and becomes a mistake only when reified as Absolute Becoming; the block picture and the evolving picture are frame-related representations, not rivals.
proof_status: Phenomenological-philosophical argument; no formal claims; note 1 states compatibility with the counterfactual-dependence explanation.
open_questions: Where exactly to draw the fixed/open line in relativistic settings (her §5 concedes the pre-reflective past/future line may be redrawn, e.g. by light cones); Newcomb and time-travel pressure cases.
relevance: The deliberative-practical candidate for the asymmetry; supplies the citation main.tex's sec:revise item needs for the record-asymmetry explanation and widens sec:direction's candidate list.
limits: Author copy; the Routledge pagination verified only via printed folios and the author's listing.

title: The Asymmetry of Influence
version: Excerpt from The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Time (Clarendon Press, Oxford; the excerpt's imprint page prints 2010; the handbook's publication year is commonly given as 2011 and was not independently verified). The excerpt itself marks that three sections are omitted.
locator: Read: §1.1 introduction (two kinds of explanation of past-directed futility; the solidity analogy); §1.2 the account's aims (static theory, passage derivative or absent); the influence/counterfactual-dependence section (photograph case; bidirectional dependence; pragmatic directionality); the counterfactual-probability machinery (fine- vs coarse-grained events, contextualized events, p¬C(E)); the omitted-sections notice; §1.3 heading.
assumptions: Dynamical laws exist; indeterminism only via chancy sources; influence = objective counterfactual probability, not compositional semantics.
conclusion: Past and future are metaphysically on par; backward influence exists in respectable senses; folk wisdom that the past is fixed arises from mistaking an asymmetry of useful influence for an asymmetry of influence simpliciter; passage, if any, is derivative on the laws plus material layout.
proof_status: Framework proposal with probabilistic machinery; the three omitted sections are stated to contain further development not audited here.
open_questions: Whether the omitted sections' decrement/ensing framework can be compared quantitatively with this repository's entropy-balance results (Prop 3/4 of the fixing-exchange note).
relevance: The pragmatic-influence candidate for the asymmetry; closest technical analogue to this repository's fixing calculus; supports sec:revise's point that the record asymmetry needs no inventory distinction.
limits: Excerpt only (three sections omitted); direct PDF retrieval through curl met a Cloudflare challenge; text was obtained through exa's extraction of the same PhilArchive item.

title: The Open Future
version: Header: 'Near Final Draft of The Open Future. Philosophy Compass, vol 6, no. 5, pp. 360-373.' Draft, not the published file.
locator: Read: §1-2 what the openness asymmetry is (against the purely epistemic reading via the amnesia case; against bivalence-defining readings; against indeterminism-defining readings, citing Lewis 1986b p. 37 and Markosian 1995; the power-over proposal and the agent-centeredness objection); §3 future ontology (ontological sense; Markosian 2008 naming); §4 branching futures and the thin red line variant (footnote 13 naming Thomason 1970 semantics); §5 OF-compatibilism vs OF-incompatibilism with Łukasiewicz 1967 p. 53, MacFarlane 2003 p. 325, Tooley 1997 pp. 44-45 quoted, and Lewis's counterfactual-dependence account quoted from Counterfactuals p. 38.
assumptions: Survey; positions presented as their holders hold them.
conclusion: The openness asymmetry is best tied to an asymmetry in power over; whether an open future is compatible with a single determinate future (OF-compatibilism) is the central question of the debate.
proof_status: Survey; quotations attributed to the originals with page numbers as given in the draft.
open_questions: Whether the power-over account is objectionably agent-centered (his own footnote 4); which asymmetric dependence grounds power-over if any.
relevance: The survey named by the task brief; organizes the asymmetry question and the OF-compatibilism taxonomy that main.tex's truth policies instantiate; source for the Lewis counterfactual-dependence and Tooley power views without reading those books.
limits: Near-final draft; end sections beyond §5 not read; quotations from Łukasiewicz, Tooley and Lewis taken on the draft's authority.

title: Compatibilism
version: First published 26 April 2004; substantive revision 16 April 2024. Entry authorship was not verified in this session and is left unnamed here.
locator: Selected sections read via HTML extraction: §1.1-1.2 classical and source incompatibilist arguments; §1.3 replies; §3.1 the Consequence Argument (power necessity, the transfer pattern, the poker example); §3.2 Frankfurt against PAP; §4.1.2-4.1.3 compatibilist replies to the Consequence Argument, naming Lewis 1981 and Slote 1982; bibliography entry for Lewis 1981, Theoria 47: 113-121.
conclusion: The Consequence Argument rests on a power-necessity transfer pattern; compatibilists either deny ability-to-do-otherwise is needed, or attack the first premise's notion of ability (Lewis), or the transfer inference (Slote).
open_questions: Which compatibilist reply is strongest; not pursued here beyond naming.
relevance: Names the standard objections to the consequence argument for READING.md part 2(c) and ranks Lewis 1981 as a next read.
limits: Only the sections named were read; entry authorship unverified.

title: Indeterminist time and truth-value gaps
version: Theoria 36 (3), December 1970, pp. 264-281; DOI 10.1111/j.1755-2567.1970.tb00427.x (verified via Crossref and the Wiley landing page). Acknowledgements on the landing page record discussions with Stalnaker and comments from van Fraassen.
locator: Landing page and metadata only; the article body is paywalled and was not read. Content known here at secondary depth: the supervaluationist clauses via Øhrstrøm & Hasle 2024 §5.4; the substitution restriction via the same entry citing Thomason 1970 p. 280; the no-true-future stance via the same entry and via Torre 2011 footnote 13 and Markosian 1995's endorsement list.
conclusion: As reported by the secondary sources read: a supervaluationist semantics for branching time on which future contingents lack truth-values while future excluded middle holds; and the objection that mixing chronicle-invariant propositional constants with chronicle-varying formulas forces restricted substitution.
proof_status: Unverified here; claims attributed to secondary readings of the primary.
open_questions: Everything at primary depth: exact clause forms, the indeterminism/no-true-future argument, the substitution discussion.
Whether an open scan exists (none found this session; Wiley paywalled).
relevance: The single most-cited primary in the area (Thomason's supervaluationism is the ancestor of main.tex policy S and of the repository's Contract S); ranked first among next reads.
limits: Discovery depth only; the paywall prevented any full-text access; all content claims rest on the labelled secondary sources.
